newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Britain must cull extra cows, Ireland says.
newsitem.headline: Britain must cull extra cows, Ireland says.

text.p: Britain must carry out an extra cull of cattle at risk to mad cow disease if the European Union is to examine exempting some British herds from a global export ban, Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates said on Monday.
"The Florence agreement has to be met. The accelerated cull has to go ahead," Yates, whose country holds the EU presidency, told reporters before the start of the farm Council.
Under a deal struck at the European Council in Florence in June, Britain must slaughter up to 147,000 extra cattle to combat the fatal cattle brain disease Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
"If that goes ahead in one part of the U.K. or Northern Ireland, then a regional proposal could be considered," Yates said, referring to grass-fed herds certified to be free of BSE.

Yates said it was up to Britain to present a plan but he believed a special case could be made for Northern Ireland because of its computerised animal identification system and because it is surrounded by water.

British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg, heading a team of five British ministers, will probe Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler's views on a regional easing of the seven-month-old EU ban on British beef exports during private talks at the meeting.
But Fischler cautioned against expecting any immediate progress.
"I don't think we will achieve very much today because I think we need more time," he told reporters before the Council.

Instead, Fischler stressed the urgent need to agree a package of measures to reduce beef production in line with a drop in demand due to consumer fears that BSE could be passed to people in the form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD).

But member states remain deeply divided over the proposed measures, which include payments to slaughter new-born calves, and fiercely oppose plans to cover the estimated 1.3 billion Ecus cost by slashing aid to cereals farmers.
Yates said a deal would be difficult and could take days.
"Certainly if we don't reach agreement we shall go very close to it here so that agreement will be in sight," he said.
